name: Nupe
notes: Nupe (Nupe-Nupe-Tako), a Nupoid (Volta-Niger, Atlantic-Congo) language of Niger and Kwara States, central Nigeria. ORTHOGRAPHY: Latin-based, 24 base letters (a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p r s t u v w y z) plus the digraphs dz, gb, kp, sh, ts and zh. Letter values that differ from a naive IPA reading: 〈c〉 = /t͡ʃ/, 〈j〉 = /d͡ʒ/, 〈y〉 = /j/, 〈sh〉 = /ʃ/, 〈zh〉 = /ʒ/, 〈ts〉 = /t͡s/, 〈dz〉 = /d͡z/, 〈gb〉 = /ɡ͡b/, 〈kp〉 = /k͡p/. Banfield & Macintyre 1915:14-16 is the source of those values; the modern digraphs sh and zh are the spellings its own notes predict for the two sounds it wrote with a dot. Vowels: oral /i e a o u/ with nasal counterparts /ĩ ẽ ã õ ũ/. RHOTIC: 〈r〉 is realised as the tap [ɾ] throughout, never the trill (Kawu 2002; Blench 2013 Nupoid overview §2), so the grapheme maps directly to /ɾ/. SECONDARY ARTICULATION (allophone_rules): Nupe has extensive labialisation and palatalisation, written consonant + 〈w〉 / consonant + 〈y〉 (Kawu 2002, ch. 3-4). A consonant immediately followed by 〈w〉/〈y〉 surfaces labialised/palatalised and the glide is absorbed (dagwa [dàɡʷā], egya [ēɡʲà]); an intervocalic 〈w〉/〈y〉 (preceded by a vowel) stays the plain glide, since it is syllabifying between two vowels rather than modifying a preceding consonant (aduwa [àdúwā], eya [èjà]). NASAL CONSONANTS AND VOWELS (allophone_rules): 〈n〉/〈m〉 split three ways by context (Kawu 2002 on Nupe nasal vowels and the syllabic nasal; Banfield & Macintyre 1915:14-15 for the nasal as an orthographic letter in its own right): (1) before a vowel, the nasal stays a plain onset consonant and the FOLLOWING vowel phonetically nasalises by post-nasal spread (ani [ānĩ́], namba [nã̀ŋ̀bà]); (2) word-final, or immediately before another nasal consonant, the nasal is silent and the PRECEDING vowel nasalises instead (dazan [dāzã̀], tanmako [tã̀mā̄kō]); (3) before an oral consonant elsewhere, the nasal surfaces as a tone-bearing syllabic nasal [ŋ] and the preceding vowel stays oral (dangi [dàŋ̀ɡī], nda [ń̀dá]). Branch (3) is the MAJORITY reading of a gold that is split on this context, not a unanimous one: of the 54 gold rows spelling a vowel + <n>/<m> + oral consonant, 30 transcribe the syllabic nasal (dangi [dàŋ̀ɡī], bindiga [bīŋ̄dīɡā]) and 24 instead nasalise the vowel and write no nasal consonant at all (gbingan [ɡ͡bĩ́ɡã̀], sanle [sã̄lē]). The split does not follow any orthographic or segmental conditioning that separates the two sets -- enangi is transcribed [ēnã̄ŋ̄ɡī], with BOTH a nasalised vowel and the syllabic nasal, while the near-identical eyangici is transcribed [ējã̄ɡítʃī] with neither -- so it is transcriber variation in the WikiPron/Wiktionary gold rather than a rule this spec could condition on. Those 24 rows are the largest single residual left once tone is folded out, and they are documented here instead of being fitted. TONE: Nupe is tonal -- three level tones plus falling and rising contours. Tone is marked with diacritics in dictionaries and careful writing (´ high, ` low, unmarked mid, ˆ/ˇ contours) but is routinely omitted in everyday text; Banfield & Macintyre 1915:17 gives that same set of marks. This spec transcribes SEGMENTS ONLY: tone diacritics are not converted into tone marks, and where tone is unwritten it is NOT RECOVERABLE from the orthography. This is a MEASURED ceiling, not a theoretical one: in the shipped wikipron/nup gold, 48 distinct Latin spellings recur with two or more different gold transcriptions, and 44 of those 48 differ only in tone/nasalisation diacritics (e.g. ebe, edu, elo, ewo), so those spellings are provably unrecoverable from segments alone. The other four are the alphabet-chart letter names <m n M N>, whose gold alternates between the letter's own sound and the syllabic nasal [ŋ]; the real-word scoring below excludes them along with the rest of the chart. Scoring only the real-word subset of that gold (excluding the alphabet-chart headwords WikiPron also carries), the segmental engine reaches PER 0.4679; folding tone diacritics out of both the hypothesis and the gold before scoring (same convention as the zom/Zou tone ceiling) drops that to PER 0.0353, which is the honest measure of how well the segmental rules perform once the genuinely unrecoverable part of the signal is set aside. INPUT CONTRACT: input is assumed to be the modern Latin (NOT Ajami) Nupe orthography, one word per token, already normalised.

sources.author: Banfield, Alexander W. and Macintyre, John Lester
sources.title: A Grammar of the Nupe Language, Together with a Vocabulary
sources.publisher: London: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge
sources.notes: Consulted directly in the full scan. Chapter I, 'The Alphabet' (pp. 14-16), is the earliest description of the letter values this orthography still carries: C is "the sound of ch in church", S-with-a-dot "the sound of sh in shut" with a note that other African languages write that sound sh, and Z-with-a-dot "the sound of z in azure, or the s in pleasure" with a note that other African languages write it zh. Its footnote (p. 16) explains that J and C are the compound sounds that would be written Dz and Ts "on strictly scientific phonetic principles", which given its z = /ʒ/ makes J the voiced palato-alveolar affricate; it also lists Dz, ts and ny as ordinary combinations. Kp and Gb are described on p. 16 as single doubly-articulated sounds, contrasted with plain p and b in the pairs kpati/pati and gboro/boro. 'The Accents' (p. 17) gives the tone marking: acute for the high tone, grave for the low, unmarked for the middle, plus a circumflex and an inverted circumflex. It writes the nasal as a distinct letter, "a strong nasal n sound as in the French word mon" (pp. 14-15).

The glide of a C+<w> sequence is absorbed once its rounding has been transferred to the preceding consonant (see NUP_LABIAL_*). An intervocalic <w> (preceded by a vowel) is untouched and stays the plain glide /w/.

The glide of a C+<y> sequence is absorbed once palatalisation has been transferred to the preceding consonant (see NUP_PALATAL_*). An intervocalic <y> (preceded by a vowel) is untouched and stays the plain glide /j/.

Orthographic word-final <n>/<m> after a vowel marks vowel nasalisation and is itself silent (Kawu 2002 on Nupe nasal vowels; Banfield & Macintyre 1915:14-15, whose nasal letter is "a strong nasal n sound as in the French word mon" rather than a coda consonant): dazan [dāzã̀], not [dāzàn].

A coda nasal immediately followed by another nasal consonant assimilates fully into it: the preceding vowel nasalises and the first nasal is silent (Kawu 2002 on Nupe nasal clusters): tanmako [tã̀mã̄kō], dinni [dĩ̀nĩ́].
